name: Tokio multi-threaded scheduler rewrite (2019)
baseline: Tokio's previous work-stealing thread pool (tokio-threadpool, the Tokio 0.1 scheduler)
verdict_reason: The rewrite did make the scheduler faster and became the default multi-threaded runtime. The '10x' headline comes from one spawn microbenchmark (12x); the other microbenchmarks improved 1.4x to 2.3x, a Hyper hello-world server 34%, and Tonic about 10%.
tier_reason: First-party blog post with benchmark output but no hardware, toolchain or build flags.
claimed_speedup: 'Some benchmarks saw a 10x speed up!' Microbenchmarks old to new: chained_spawn 2,019,796 to 168,854 ns/iter, ping_pong 1,279,948 to 562,659, spawn_many 10,283,608 to 7,320,737, yield_many 21,450,748 to 14,638,563 (12.0x, 2.3x, 1.4x and 1.5x, derived from page data). Hyper hello world: 113923.19 to 152258.70 requests/sec, 'an increase of 34%'; Tonic 'about a 10% speed up'.
workload: Tokio scheduler microbenchmarks (recursive spawning, ping-pong messaging, spawning many tasks, frequent yields), plus a Hyper hello-world server under wrk -t1 -c50 -d10.
one_liner: Tokio's 2019 scheduler rewrite, the basis of its multi-threaded runtime since 0.2; 12x on one microbenchmark, 34% on a Hyper server.
how_it_is_fast: Each worker owns a local run queue that idle workers steal from, and the number of workers searching for work at once is throttled so idle threads do not all contend. A task woken by a message goes into a 'next task' slot and runs next, while the message is still in cache. Task structures were reworked to cut allocations and atomic reference counting.
use_it_when: The default for async Rust: the numbers describe the scheduler you already get from Tokio's multi-threaded runtime
skip_it_when: Comparing against runtimes benchmarked before late 2019, which measured the old scheduler
caveats: No hardware, OS or compiler flags stated.
The 10x figure is from a single microbenchmark; end-to-end gains were 10-34%.
Benchmarks are from 2019; the scheduler has changed again since (for example cooperative budgeting in 2020).
tradeoffs: Work stealing requires tasks to be Send, unlike thread-per-core runtimes.

evidence.quote: Some benchmarks saw a 10x speed up!
an increase of 34% requests per second just from switching schedulers!
